parts.label: (a)
hints: Hint 1: Think of the first law as energy conservation for the gas - internal energy can only increase if energy is put in from outside in one of two distinct ways.
Hint 2: Remember the sign convention here: + means energy added TO the system, so link +q to heating and +w to compression by an external force.
parts.proper_answer: +q is the thermal energy transferred to the system; +w is the work done on the system.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What the first law means**
Think of the gas as your system. Its internal energy $\Delta U$ is the sum of random kinetic energies of its molecules. It can only increase if energy flows in from the surroundings.

Step 2: **The two routes in**
There are only two routes: heating and mechanical work. So $$\Delta U = (+q) + (+w)$$ where $+q$ is thermal energy transferred TO the system, and $+w$ is work done ON the system by an external agent compressing it. A negative value would mean energy leaving the system.

parts.label: (b)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Look at the line A to B in Fig. 2.1 - what quantity stays constant while the volume changes from $2.3 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}^3$ to $3.8 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}^3$?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Spot constant pressure expansion**
A to B is vertical on the $V$ against $p$ graph, so pressure $p$ is constant at $2.6 \times 10^{5}\text{ Pa}$ while volume increases. The gas expands and does work on the surroundings.

Step 2: **Calculate $p\Delta V$**
For constant pressure: $$W = p\Delta V$$ $$W = 2.6 \times 10^{5} \times (3.8 \times 10^{-3} - 2.3 \times 10^{-3})$$ $$W = 2.6 \times 10^{5} \times 1.5 \times 10^{-3} = 390\text{ J}$$ This is the magnitude of work done by the gas.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Focus on the word cycle - compare the starting state A with the final state after A to B to C to A.
Hint 2: Recall what determines the internal energy of a fixed mass of ideal gas, and whether that quantity is different at the end of a full loop.
parts.proper_answer: No total change in internal energy. The gas returns to its original state and original temperature, and $U$ of an ideal gas depends only on temperature.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Internal energy depends only on state**
For a fixed mass of ideal gas, internal energy $U$ depends only on temperature $T$. It does not depend on the path taken. It is a state function.

Step 2: **Complete cycle means no net change**
In one complete cycle the gas starts at A and finishes back at A, so $p$, $V$ and $T$ are all the same as at the start. Therefore $$\Delta U_{total} = 0$$ There is no net change in internal energy.

parts.label: (c)
hints: Hint 1: Start with A to B - you are given heat in, and you found work magnitude in (b)(i), but decide the sign of $w$ carefully: is work done on the gas or by the gas during expansion?
Hint 2: For B to C, use the clue that no thermal energy enters or leaves - what does that tell you about $q$, and how does $\Delta U$ then relate to the given $w = +550\text{ J}$?
Hint 3: For the whole cycle, combine your result from (b)(ii) that total $\Delta U = 0$ to find the missing $\Delta U$ for C to A.
Hint 4: For C to A, look at Fig. 2.1 - volume is constant at $2.3 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}^3$, so what must $w$ be, and then use $\Delta U = q + w$ to find $q$?
parts.proper_answer: A to B: $q = +1370\text{ J}$, $w = -390\text{ J}$, $\Delta U = +980\text{ J}$; B to C: $q = 0$, $w = +550\text{ J}$, $\Delta U = +550\text{ J}$; C to A: $q = -1530\text{ J}$, $w = 0$, $\Delta U = -1530\text{ J}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **A to B - heated expansion**
$q = +1370\text{ J}$ is given as heat TO the gas. Expansion means work is done BY the gas, so work done ON the gas is negative: $w = -390\text{ J}$. Apply the first law: $$\Delta U = q + w = 1370 - 390 = +980\text{ J}$$

Step 2: **B to C - adiabatic compression**
No thermal transfer means $q = 0$. Work done ON the gas is given as $+550\text{ J}$, so $w = +550\text{ J}$. Then: $$\Delta U = 0 + 550 = +550\text{ J}$$

Step 3: **Use the cycle condition for C to A**
Total $\Delta U$ over the cycle is zero from (b)(ii): $$980 + 550 + \Delta U_{CA} = 0$$ $$\Delta U_{CA} = -1530\text{ J}$$

Step 4: **C to A - constant volume cooling**
C to A is horizontal on Fig. 2.1 at $V = 2.3 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}^3$. No volume change means no work: $w = 0$. Then: $$q = \Delta U - w = -1530 - 0 = -1530\text{ J}$$ Heat is lost by the gas as pressure falls at constant volume.
